item.title: US Project Vault readies $1B loan blitz for industry
item.description: Federal-backed financing aims to help US manufacturers secure essential metals and materials amid supply risks.
item.dc:creator: Cecilia Jamasmie
item.content:encoded:
US Project Vault readies $1B loan blitz for industry

Staff Writer | October 16, 2026 | 5:39 am Battery Metals   Critical Minerals   Suppliers & Equipment   Africa   USA   Cobalt   Copper   Lithium   Nickel   Rare Earth   Specialty Minerals

Trump addressing coal industry representatives. ( Image courtesy of The White House. )

The US government-backed Project Vault is preparing to issue up to $1 billion in loans to American manufacturers seeking critical minerals, advancing Washington’s efforts to shield domestic industry from supply disruptions.

VaultCo, the entity managing the stockpiling initiative, is in discussions with more than 70 companies across the critical minerals supply chain, Bloomberg reported . The first round of financing is expected to cover more than a dozen original equipment manufacturers (OEMs), with another group to follow.

“What’s likely to happen is we’ll announce several hundred million dollars, maybe a billion dollars, of loans to OEMs who have requested use of the Vault facility,” VaultCo Executive Chairman Brett Lambert told the news outlet. “In the first tranche, we’ll have more than a dozen firms, followed by more than a dozen shortly after.”

The financing would mark a significant step towards making Project Vault operational as the US seeks to reduce its exposure to volatile critical minerals markets and strengthen manufacturers’ access to materials essential for industrial production.

Trump launches $12B ‘Project Vault’ to cut China reliance

Lambert said the recipients would not be publicly identified at this stage, although the announcement is expected to disclose the types of minerals they have requested.

Stockpile takes shape

Launched in February , Project Vault is structured as an independently governed public-private partnership backed by a $10 billion loan from the US Export-Import Bank (EXIM) and nearly $2 billion in private investment.

Commodity trading giants Glencore (LON: GLEN) and Mercuria recently committed $500 million each , becoming the first commodity traders to join the initiative.

Mercuria has already delivered 12,000 tonnes of copper from the Democratic Republic of Congo , establishing a new destination for the African country’s metal within Washington’s supply security strategy.

Glencore, Mercuria to help build US minerals stockpile with $1B EXIM financing

The shipment comes amid growing US demand for Congolese copper. Imports reached a record 53,290 tonnes in July, driven by competitive prices, improved product quality and concerns over potential tariffs that prompted buyers to accelerate shipments.

Commercial imports and Project Vault serve different purposes. While conventional purchases meet immediate industrial demand, the reserve is intended to provide manufacturers with access to materials when normal supply channels become disrupted.

Tailored mineral demand

Unlike conventional government stockpiles, Project Vault is designed around manufacturers’ specific requirements rather than predetermined inventories of strategic commodities.

Participating companies have requested not only raw metals and minerals but also specialized magnets, powders, alloys and other processed materials tailored to their production needs.

“There isn’t any one mineral that stands out, but the specificity of the requests have surprised me,” Lambert told Bloomberg .

The demand-driven approach allows manufacturers to determine which materials are purchased and stored, potentially giving smaller buyers greater purchasing power in fragmented and often opaque markets.

Op-Ed: US has built a strategic copper reserve. Now can it keep it?

It also distinguishes Project Vault from the US National Defense Stockpile , which the Defense Logistics Agency administers to secure materials required for national defence.

The next test will be whether the initial loans can translate manufacturers’ highly specific requests into reliable inventories, particularly for processed materials that may be harder to source than raw commodities.

item.title: Tech giants come knocking for a piece of Anglo American as copper scarcity bites, Wanblad tells FT
item.description: Wanblad says "deep expressions of interest" from tech companies have yet to turn into a stake, while Beijing holds the key to the $54 billion Teck merger.
item.dc:creator: Frik Els
item.content:encoded:
Tech giants come knocking for a piece of Anglo American as copper scarcity bites, Wanblad tells FT

Frik Els | October 15, 2026 | 10:55 am Markets   Top Companies   Africa   Australia   Canada   China   Latin America   Copper   Diamond   Nickel   Palladium   Platinum

Los Bronces copper mine in Chile. ( Image courtesy of Anglo American | Flickr. )

Anglo American (LON: AAL) has held talks with technology companies interested in buying equity in the miner as a way of securing supplies of the metals that go into data centres, chief executive Duncan Wanblad told the Financial Times’ Metals and Mining Summit in London on Thursday.

Discussions were “absolutely being had”, Wanblad said, with the question from the tech side coming down to whether to lock in long-term offtake directly or take an equity position to secure a stake in future supply. No stakes have been taken, but there had been “deep expressions of interest” in doing so, he told the summit. “Given the scarcity issue that we’ve been speaking about, a lot of people are looking for ways to secure supply.”

Comex copper for December delivery traded near $6.52 a pound (about $14,370 a tonne) on Thursday, a third straight decline, after stronger than expected US inflation data put a Federal Reserve rate hike this month back on the table. Cash copper on the LME settled at a record $14,822 on Monday and the most-active Comex contract remains within 6% of its September 9 record settlement of $6.89.

A $90 billion copper company

Anglo’s New York-listed shares added 0.6% to $26.86 in early trade on Thursday for a market value of $58.0 billion, while Teck Resources (NYSE: TECK) edged up 0.3% to $64.96 and is worth $31.9 billion. At those prices Anglo-Teck would carry a combined nominal value of just under $90 billion, up from the $53 billion the two companies put on the merger of equals when it was announced in September last year .

Teck has been the better performer since, gaining 50% over the past 12 months against 36% for Anglo, and both are among the strongest diversified miners of 2026. The combination would rank alongside Glencore at $89 billion and Freeport-McMoRan at $99 billion.

Waiting on Beijing

The approaches come while Anglo waits on China for the final clearance on the merger with Teck, a combination that would rank among the five largest copper producers with annual output of about 1.2 million tonnes. Wanblad would not be drawn at the summit on what Chinese regulators want in return for approval, according to the FT.

China’s State Administration for Market Regulation has asked Anglo to commit to a steady flow of copper concentrate to Chinese smelters, including volumes sold through traders, as a condition for clearing the deal, Reuters reported on October 2. The remedies under discussion do not include asset sales. The combined group would control around 5% of global copper supply, well below the 10% to 15% thresholds that normally trigger competition concerns, but China refines up to 60% of the world’s copper cathode and is facing its worst feedstock shortage in decades. Canada , the EU , the US, Japan, Chile and South Korea have all signed off, and the parties still expect to close by March 2027.

Wanblad said in August that mining transactions now take “probably a little bit longer than they might have done five years ago”, with companies needing to allow 12 to 18 months for approvals , while rejecting the idea that regulation was making deals impossible to get done.

Nickel closure on the table

Anglo is also likely to shut its nickel business in Brazil if the European Union does not approve the planned $500 million sale of the assets to China’s MMG, Wanblad told the conference. The European Commission opened an in-depth probe of the deal late last year over fears MMG could divert ferronickel from Codemin and Barro Alto away from European stainless steel makers, and issued a formal warning last month. MMG has since proposed long-term European supply commitments .

Anglo’s Brazil chief operating officer Ruben Fernandes told a closed hearing in Brussels last week that MMG was the only credible buyer the company had identified and that a prohibition would leave it heading for care and maintenance as the pathway to closure.

The nickel sale and the Teck merger are the two remaining pieces of a portfolio simplification that also has Anglo seeking about $1 billion for De Beers .

item.title: Copper price forecasts lifted for 2026 but tariff “collapse” still on the table
item.description: Macquarie’s collapse scenario needs Washington to rule tariffs out, which it rates least likely. More likely is limbo past January 1, with 1.5 million tonnes of US copper staying exactly where it is.
item.dc:creator: Frik Els
item.content:encoded:
Copper price forecasts lifted for 2026 but tariff “collapse” still on the table

Staff Writer | October 14, 2026 | 9:31 am Critical Minerals   Markets   China   Latin America   USA   Copper

Where do we send these? Credit: Glencore

Copper pulled back from a three-week high on Wednesday after US inflation data put a Federal Reserve rate hike this month back on the table, and word of a preliminary deal to avert a strike at BHP’s Escondida, the world’s largest copper mine, took some of the supply premium out of the price.

Comex copper for December delivery traded at $6.6695 a pound (about $14,704 a tonne) late morning in New York, down 0.8%, after touching $6.7890 earlier in the session. The most-active contract’s record settlement of $6.89 was set on September 9 , the day before a report that the White House tariff plan had stalled knocked more than 5% off the price.

In London, three-month copper climbed as far as $14,700 a tonne, its highest since September 23, before easing to $14,532 by early afternoon. Cash copper settled at a record $14,822 on Monday and $14,741 on Tuesday, and LME inventories have fallen for seven straight sessions to 229,650 tonnes.

US consumer prices accelerated in September on a surge in gasoline costs, and the CME’s FedWatch tool put the odds of a quarter-point hike at the Fed’s late-October meeting at about 44%, double the day before, Reuters reported. New York Fed President John Williams said he still sees one more hike this year.

Two sources told Reuters that Escondida’s supervisors’ union and the company had reached a preliminary agreement , which members were voting on Wednesday morning, and a union leader told Bloomberg a deal was “virtually done”. Unions at Antofagasta’s Centinela returned to talks on Tuesday after a week-long stoppage, while the open pit at Codelco’s El Teniente remains shut after a deadly landslide .

Click on chart for live prices.

Copper’s 2026 advance has forecasters raising their numbers for the second time in three months, and with the metal averaging $13,471 a tonne for the year to date, the 2026 revisions mostly bring the sheet into line with the tape.

Macquarie now has copper averaging $13,573 this year, BMO Capital Markets $13,619 and BMI, a unit of Fitch Solutions, $13,500, up from the $12,700 it moved to in July . The differences open up from next year, and they come down to how much of the 1.5 to 2 million tonnes of copper now sitting in the United States is counted as surplus.

“The great copper gamble”

Macquarie, which in July called the rally “running ahead of reality” , has lifted its 2027 average by 14% to $12,750 and pushed the cycle low to $12,000 in the fourth quarter of next year from $11,000 a quarter earlier, while its long-term price rises to $10,500 a tonne in 2025 dollars.

Prices “have disconnected from the fundamentals and could arguably move higher or lower depending on the outcome of the Section 232,” the bank’s strategists write in a quarterly compendium whose copper chapter is headed “The great copper gamble”, listing the metal among its preferred commodities for the next six to nine months “but very binary”.

The fundamentals as Macquarie counts them are a 223,000-tonne surplus this year after a 531,000-tonne disruption allowance, and surpluses averaging more than 700,000 tonnes a year from 2027 as mine supply grows 4.9% next year and 4.3% in 2028, with Collahuasi, Grasberg, Kamoa-Kakula and Centinela ramping up, Tia Maria starting and Cobre Panama back in full from mid-2027.

Global demand growth slows to 1.5% in 2027 on its numbers, with none at all in China, where construction-related copper use is shrinking 9% a year and air conditioner makers are “again looking at aluminium substitution.”

Visible stocks worldwide are up 300,000 tonnes this year, but that is the US build; everywhere else they are down 168,000 tonnes, and Macquarie says sentiment will not turn until LME and Shanghai inventories start rising again, either quickly on a tariff decision or gradually as its forecast surpluses feed through.

Macquarie’s four tariff scenarios run from a January 1 that passes with no announcement at all, which it rates most likely, to a definitive decision against a duty, which it rates least likely: “the CME price will most likely collapse, taking the LME price with it, and the arb will invert,” with surplus US stocks reappearing in LME warehouses in the US and Asia.

A tariff announced six to eight weeks ahead of implementation would pull a last wave of metal into the US and leave the rest of the world “very tight”, while a formal six-month delay would see the spread fade as it did for platinum and palladium after the critical minerals decision.

Expectations are also growing that a scrap export ban will be folded into any decision; an immediate ban would take about 600,000 tonnes a year of contained copper off the world market.

“Has the market misread US inventory?”

BMO Capital Markets arrives at a very different place from a similar starting point. Its quarterly price deck, published two days before Macquarie’s, raises its long-term copper price by 47% to $16,000 a tonne in real terms, or $18,000 nominal by 2030, with $14,675 for 2027 and $16,000 for 2028, and the bank puts itself 46% above consensus on the long-term number. Its market balance is close to balanced throughout: an 83,000-tonne surplus this year, then small deficits from 2027.

The argument turns on what the US hoard, now close to 2 million tonnes on BMO’s estimate, or about a year of American consumption, actually represents. China’s refined copper imports have run below trend and its exports above trend since the tariff trade began, a cumulative swing of about 1.6 million tonnes on a net basis, which BMO reads as Beijing allowing its strategic reserve to run down while Washington built one.

“Instead of there being a build in above ground inventory over the last 2 years, there has been a geographical redistribution from ‘not visible’ to ‘visible’, meaning today’s price of ~$14,500-15,000/t is fundamentally supported,” the bank writes. Had China bid for metal alongside the US, “copper prices today would in fact be much, much higher,” and at some point China will want to restock.

BMO expects no tariff decision before the US midterms in November, which may see copper “pause for breath” and keep the Comex-LME spread narrow, but says investors it talks to are coming around to the view that the US stockpile “could simply stay in situ for many more years.”

Rising dependence on scrap, with China’s secondary refined output heading for 3.3 million tonnes this year from 2.8 million, is the other leg of its case: scrap is the marginal unit, and it only comes out at higher prices.

BMI sits between the two. It still views the rally “as having extended beyond what fundamentals alone would suggest” and has the market in a 43,000-tonne surplus this year, but has cut its 2026 mine supply growth forecast to 1.1% from 2.4% with Chilean output down 4%, and expects a deficit from 2027 that widens to 1.7 million tonnes by 2035 as demand grows 3% to 4% a year on grids, EVs and data centres.

Its 2027 forecast is $12,900, rising to $15,000 in 2029 and an unchanged $17,000 in 2035. The International Copper Study Group, meeting this week, lifted its 2026 surplus to 104,000 tonnes and kept 2027 at 368,000 tonnes.

The arb has gone, the metal has not

The spread that built the US stockpile has all but disappeared on a spot basis. Comex October copper at $6.62 a pound trades below LME cash, which at Tuesday’s $14,741 works out to $6.69, and John Gross of The Copper Journal calculates the month-to-date average has flipped to an 85-point LME premium from a 17-cent Comex premium in June.

Most of that is London’s doing: the backwardation that put cash $164.50 over three months at Monday’s settlement, since narrowed to $115.50, reflects how little spot metal is left outside the US.

Aurubis, Europe’s largest copper producer, has offered customers a record premium of $347 a tonne for 2027 supply, 10% above this year’s level, Benchmark Minerals reported, and a company spokesperson told Bloomberg that “a lot of material has relocated to the US, leaving warehouses quite empty.”

Further down the curve the premium survives. December Comex at $14,704 a tonne sits about $170 over LME three-month, which Macquarie read at the end of September as the market pricing a 10% chance of a 15% duty (on Wednesday’s prices the same arithmetic gives about 8%).

That is too little to pull fresh shipments across the Atlantic, but enough to keep what is already there in place as long as the Comex curve pays traders to hold it. The tonnes still arriving are cargo booked months ago: Comex stocks rose another 6,500 tonnes last week to 713,000 tonnes, with 100,000 tonnes of African and South American copper due through October.

Deutsche Bank takes the stockpiling argument furthest. Daniel Ghali, the bank’s new head of metals research, told the Wall Street Journal that with China adding to its strategic reserve for decades and the tariff threat pulling metal into American sheds, the two countries could be sitting on 71% of the world’s supply by the end of the year. On that trajectory copper “simply won’t be available” to users elsewhere by the end of 2028, an outcome averted only by prices high enough to force substitution into aluminium.

He sees $10 a pound, or $22,050 a tonne, in the second quarter of 2027, almost 50% above current levels. Even a decision against tariffs may not free the metal, he told the paper, since the LME has warehouses in the US and copper may simply be shuffled between American sites rather than leave the country.

Gross points to copper’s premium over aluminium, which hit a record $5.08 a pound in September, more than double its July 2022 low. “Clearly, this rising premium cannot continue indefinitely, but who among us will step forward to say it’s at the top?” he writes. His September monthly report makes the longer point: China consumed 58.9% of the world’s refined copper last year, up from 12.4% in 2000. “There are too many copper eggs in China’s basket.”

Miners still pricing $5 copper

Copper producers fell with the metal on Wednesday, Lundin Mining down 3.9%, Freeport-McMoRan 3.7%, Southern Copper 3.3% and Teck Resources 2.9%, but the year has been kind. Southern Copper is up 44.1% in 2026, taking its market value to $169 billion, with Glencore ahead 38.6%, BHP 38.0% and Freeport 37.4% at a $100 billion valuation. Teck has gained 36.1% and Anglo American 29.2%. Lundin has managed 13.0%, Antofagasta 7.5% with Centinela on strike, and First Quantum 3.0%.

RBC Capital Markets calculates that North American copper producers at 1.0 times net asset value imply a copper price of $5.03 a pound, from $5.98 for Freeport down to $3.96 for Ivanhoe Mines, against a futures price near $6.70. The group trades at 0.9 times net asset value, in line with its 10-year average.

Comex copper is up more than 18% in 2026.
